utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett, Thomas Laugel, and legal intern Pape Malick Djiba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please us your name, first name, name, date of birth, and -- yeah, and your nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frederick Noseworthy, born 13 June 1948. Nationality Canadian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it your testimony will be in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oui. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Noseworthy, you're about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now please read the solemn declaration the usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Gillett, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, good morning. Can you hear me loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I see you have a document in front of you. Could you tell the Court what that document is?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That's the -- this is my sworn statement. And the affidavit, the witness statement just so that I can remind myself what I said if need be, and I think the Court has this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the usher would like to show the document to the Defence, we're fine with that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you please tell the Chamber when you first arrived in the former Yugoslavia to carry out your duty with the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I arrived on the morning of September the 7th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what was your role with the mission, I'll call it the ECMM, as I ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I was the commander of the Canadian contingent to the ECMM and I was the Chief Operations Officer for the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now in relation to the statement in front of you, did you provide a statement to the Prosecution of this Tribunal in 2012?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I'd ask that 65 ter document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to pause between question and answer for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll observe a pause after your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter document 06379 be placed on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the document on the monitor, do you recognise that to be the statement that you gave and do you recognise your signature at the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I don't see my signature on this. But I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Perhaps if we zoom on the English version, and if we scroll to the next page?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you arrived in The Hague this week to testify, were you given a chance to review your statement and make any corrections?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of the statement?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you were asked about the same matters today, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I hope so. Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter document 6379 together with the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just want to make a comment here that my -- my responses to these questions are based on memory from 21, 22 years ago, so detail is -- is difficult to draw upon, but having read -- read the statement that I gave initially, I'm confident that my answers were as accurate as they could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's -- it is reassuring, sir, that you're not claiming to remember everything from 20 years ago. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2891. And the associated documents shall be assigned exhibit numbers to be circulated to the parties at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you some questions about some additional documents that relate to matters addressed in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could first get 65 ter document 1269 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, this fax and the attached summary concern a meeting of the joint commission of 20 September 1992. Could you tell the Chamber what the joint commission was?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: The joint commission was a -- was a conference structure set up by the United Nations, which included the European Community Monitor Mission of which I was a member, and the two opposing -- or representatives from the two opposing factions to try and resolve the issue of the pink -- what was known then as the pink zones, which was a zone of -- zone of contention between the official cease-fire line and the zones which were protected by the United Nations forces, the UN -- the United Nations Protected Areas, UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could go to the final page of this document, and on this page, under ECMM, we see that your name is listed as the third person. Does that mean that you attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I did. I also want to point out that the voice of the mission, of the European Community Monitoring Mission was Ambassador John MacDonald from the United Kingdom. I was there as Chief Operations Officer to advise him on operational matters. My input into those meetings, any meetings that I attended, were strictly related to ECMM operations modus operandi and what was reported through our reporting system, but I didn't -- I -- I didn't speak on behalf of the mission. I was an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to page 2 of this document and if we look at the first paragraph, it states that the joint commission was established to oversee the step by step restoration of Croatian authority in pink zones. You've described what the pink zones are. Now putting aside what was supposed to happen under Resolution 762, who actually controlled the pink zones on the ground at this time?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It was in contention the -- the Croatian forces, Croatian government, sought to re-establish complete sovereignty over the pink zones, while the ethnic Serb faction, population, at the time, and it's my understanding of the intention at the time, wished to retain control over it for themselves. That was the -- that was the essence of the conflict and the -- the joint -- the objective of the joint commission was to get the two opposing factions to talk to each other so that we could resolve that and do away with the pink zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we move to page 3 in the second paragraph, the document states that Cedric Thornberry met with Martic, Spanovic, and Zivkovic, and they agreed to the disarmament of the special police by 15 October 1992. Did that disarmament occur as agreed?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Not my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what effect did the presence of these heavily armed special police have on the non-Serb population in the UNPAs and the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by the term "special police." They were paramilitaries, and the effect of having heavily armed paramilitaries in the zone was an intimidation. It was intimidation to the population, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2892. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might intervene before you go further, Mr. Gillett. Mr. Noseworthy, going back to your answer that appears at line 13, "the objective the joint commission was to get the two opposing factions to talk to each other so that we could resolve that and do away with the pink zones." That answer, in part, answers something that I was curious about, namely as to -- if you have the -- these demarcation lines and the UNPAs, how come the pink zones came about? But the question I want to pose now is whether these were -- these pink zones had, as it were, fixed boundaries or were they sort of -- having regard to the conflicts of which you speak, whether they were floating areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were reasonably well defined because there was a fixed cease-fire line and that's where they -- the official conflict ended. But there were -- there were areas that the United Nations had inserted -- what's called the United Nations Protection Force, they were at UNPAs, those areas didn't coincide exactly with the -- the cease-fire line. So you had this zone in between the two in which -- which was -- which was contested. I'm sorry if that doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think I understand. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could now get 65 ter document 1361. And this again -- 1351, apologies. And this again concerns the work of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now this fax and the attached summary concern a meeting of the joint commission on 9 November 1992. If we turn to the final page, page 7, we see an individual listed under the ECMM called Patrick Curley? Who was Patrick Curley?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Patrick Curley was an Irish officer, a lieutenant-colonel in the Irish army. He was the commander of the Irish contingent to the European Community Monitor Mission and he worked for me as one of my staff officers. I was not able to attend the joint commission on that day. I was away on a mission myself and I assigned Patrick Curley to attend in my stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Patrick Curley inform you of the contents of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: He sure did. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we look at page 1 of this document, we see that the meetings of the joint commission were adjourned without a fixed date for a subsequent meeting and the writer of the fax, Cedric Thornberry, states in the last line of this front page that the Serb side is substantially responsible for the UNPAs. How did the Serb side stand to benefit by impeding the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know, it wasn't just the Serb side. There were both sides -- were -- were stalling the -- the progress here. But by -- by stalling, they were trading time for influence, I suppose. The -- I know that Cedric Thornberry was extremely frustrated by this time, and -- and the -- the two sides weren't prepared to talk to each other at all, which was the purpose of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you say "they were trading time for influence," could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, yeah, the -- I mean, yes. By agreeing to meet with -- in -- in the form of the joint commission, it would appear to the world that they were co-operating in the -- in the effort to resolve the issue of the -- of the pink zones. But, at the same time, there were paramilitaries roaming the country-side, and they weren't just roaming this was, in my view, organised, and they were intimidating populations. And it was -- in retrospect it would like now as though by stalling for time, in -- in -- they could probably establish themselves as the dominant force in -- in that zone and the Croatian government was getting very, very frustrated. Because, in their view it was clearly -- in fact, the pink zones in -- in the context of what they were -- were recognised as Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you refer to these organised paramilitaries, what terms were used to describe them?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: In English they were called special police. In practical terms, they were a militia, a paramilitary militia. They were irregulars. They were organised. They operated as -- as an organised militia - again, that's my term - but an organised paramilitary unit. But they were called special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What type of equipment did these units have?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Ah. I personally only saw side-arms and assault weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you read reports of them having any other equipment?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What type of equipment?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know something? I can't -- I just cannot remember the detail. I'd have to read the reports again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to give a general answer or not?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah. They had -- in -- as I recall, they had what would be considered as -- as infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you could --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: A broad spectrum of infantry weapons. Crew-served weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you explain what crew-served weapons are?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, a crew-served weapon is any weapon that requires more than one person to operate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you give an example?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah. A machine-gun is a crew-served weapon if it is belt fed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender 65 ter document 1351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2893. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And my final question. In your statement at paragraph 63, you state that Goran Hadzic was the president of the RSK and that you ran into him in Knin at one point in time. Could you describe what occurred during that encounter?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It was a very brief -- I'm sorry, I should wait. It was a very, very brief encounter. I was with a member of the Knin co-ordinating centre for the European Community Monitor Mission. He was my guide. I used to visit the -- the various teams and coordinating centres and regional centres around the deployment area. It was part of my duties. I was their immediate superior, and I was being given a tour of the area. We were in a government building, and Mr. Hadzic and I just essentially crossed paths, and it was a very brief encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: How did you know he was president of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: My guide told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else about Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It's one of those things you don't forget. And he -- he stated to me that not much goes on in this area that he doesn't know about, I think, was his -- as best as I can summarise the statement. I tried to -- and I should say to the Court that I tried to reconfirm that issue. The officer who was -- who was escorting me at the time is suffering post-traumatic stress disorder. I was not able to speak to him so that is the -- that is the exchange in the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gillett. Is the Defence ready for cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Zivanovic, if you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I consult my client for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Noseworthy. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and I am counsel for Mr. Goran Hadzic in this case. I would like to discuss two topics in your testimony, the first being demilitarisation. As you testified, you began your work with ECMM on 7th of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And before that you had two weeks of preparatory work, briefings?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And through those briefings, did you learn the historical background and recent developments in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know I have to be honest, not in the detail that I would have preferred, but we had a -- we had a lot of briefings, and we were exposed to individuals who had lived in the former Yugoslavia who gave us historical briefings and gave us some history of the area. We were also -- went through a short training period when we arrive in the mission. That was perhaps much more relevant to the mission itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were aware of the details of Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first phase of -- of this plan was demilitarisation and withdrawal of the JNA. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: As I understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have Rule 65 ter exhibit 1402.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a book from Colonel Riley as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the page 7 in e-court, please. It is in penultimate paragraph on the left side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence reads: "ECMM teams also monitored the withdrawal of the JNA out of Krajina which began in May 1992, having been permitted to enter Krajina in April." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next page of this document, it is the first -- I think it is the first paragraph and first sentence read: "The cease-fire in Croatian was broken in May by Croatian army attacks north of Split." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: The actual event, I don't recall it. But it's part of the history of the -- of the conflict. So, yes, I'm aware of it. I was not in theatre in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you are aware that in the first week of June 1992, the Croatian army invaded Bosnia and Herzegovina and cut off the corridor connecting RSK with former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That's -- that's a matter of history, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that the corridor was vital for survival of the RSK? This connection between Yugoslavia on one side, and the RSK on the other.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah. It's -- that is -- the answer is yes, if -- if RSK was to be accepted as a -- as a viable entity. But I'm not sure -- I must say I'm not sure that in international law that that was -- that's universally accepted. But from the perspective of the population of the -- the ethnic Serb population within the RSK, that would have to be the way that they would have viewed the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're aware that the corridor was re-established only after the armed intervention of the RSK forces in first part of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that on 21st of June, 1992, the Croatian army made an incursion into the Miljevacki Plateau, in contravention of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It is a matter of history. I was not in theatre at the time. So the answer is: I did not observe any of this, but it is -- it -- it's a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you confirm that the RSK forces halted the Croatian's army incursion into Miljevacki Plateau?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It's a matter of history. It's a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the UN Security Council's Resolution 762 condemning these acts of Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now please -- would you agree that if the RSK had continued disarming its forces, it would not have been able to resist to these and the future acts of Croatia -- Croats?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You're asking me for an opinion that -- that I'm not comfortable in giving because the situation that you're describing is a -- is a situation that wasn't universally accepted as being legitimate. But from the view of the RSK, I have to -- I have to concede, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that on 22nd of January, 1993, the Croatian army attacked the Maslenica region?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And if the RSK had not its armed forces, they could not resist to this attack. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that UN Security Council passed the Resolution 802, condemning these attacks and calling on Croatia to withdraw its forces to previous confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Can I comment on that? Because there was much -- there was much activity going on back and forth, and there were United Nations Council's resolutions, there was demarches, diplomatic notes were being exchanged all the time because there were -- it was a very fluid situation. I just wanted to put that in the context. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that Croatia refused to comply with the resolution?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And, indeed, Croatia continued its action by shelling Serb positions in the Kordun region?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in September 1993, the Croatian army launched an attack on Medak pocket where they committed crimes against Serb civilian population?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Again, now you're asking me questions that post-date my -- my service in the -- in the theatre. But, of course, I'm well aware of it. There was a Canadian battalion that was involved in that activity, and yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you might be aware that the military leaders responsible for this attack were indicted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that if the RSK did not have its armed formations, they could not resist this attack?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: No, because in the Medak pocket, if you recall, there was a major -- well, in terms of the activities that were going on at the time, but there was a major confrontation between the Canadian battalion, which was a member of the United Nations Protection Force, and the Croatian forces. I'm speaking now from -- from a historical perspective. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you confirm that the Serb population in RSK did not see any effective measures undertaken by UNPROFOR to deter Croatia from armed attacks --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, if we go back --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- of UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we go back to that one particular example that you're using of the Medak pocket, the United Nations Protection Force did offer stiff resistance against the Croatian forces to protect the Serb population. Just an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I repeat my last question. Could you confirm that the Serb population in RSK did not see any effective measure undertaken by UNPROFOR to deter Croatia from armed attacks on UN protection areas?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know, I can't -- I can't answer that question because I wasn't a part of the Serb population and I'm looking it from the outside as a -- as a third party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have in -- just in this book. I read the statement, but I'm not able to find it right now, but ... on that -- maybe you can recall. That the Serb population distrust in UNPROFOR -- have distrust in -- had distrust in UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: In the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In RSK.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that's -- that's a fact. The Serb population felt threatened, and they did express displeasure with UNPROFOR and that's a matter of history. That's a historical fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree in light of these attacks, that the Serb population might perceive the insistence that the Serb -- Serbs disarm resemble the policy that would facilitate Croatian military occupation of the UN protection areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, the witness is being asked to speculate on the subjective viewpoints of other persons. He said he was looking from a different person, so I just note that in relation to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as a monitor, as -- as a European Community Monitor Mission operator, I would have to say that from our perspective, we -- we were there to monitor the conflict and to -- and to observe that the laws of armed conflict were being respected and I cannot comment on what one faction or the other felt. I can only comment on whether or not the -- their activities, their armed activities were being carried out in accordance with the laws of armed conflict. As I understood them. And so if one faction or another conducted operations that were not in accordance with the laws of armed conflict, then it was our duty to report that and the result of those reports is bearing out in -- in this courtroom right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your communication with the people, did you see any distrust in UNPROFOR intentions?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: And the answer to that is an unqualified yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another topic, and that is the resettlement of displaced persons and refugees. You were aware of the large number of Croats displaced from UN Protected Areas East, South, and North. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the large number of Serbs displaced from Western Slavonia, UN Protected Area of west --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the whole area was -- was affected by the displacement of -- of citizens from one location to another, based on their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And most of population from Western Slavonia -- most of Serb population from Western Slavonia were temporarily settled in Eastern Slavonia, in UNP East. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: As I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, the Vance Plan provided for the return of displaced persons and refugees to their homes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw documents today which indicated ECMM widely discussed the return of Croat refugees to Sector East.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they would return to houses temporarily occupied by the refugees from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That did happen, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you can see from these document, the return of refugees from Western Slavonia to their homes elsewhere was not discussed at all. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that -- that they were not discussed at all. The issue of displaced persons was a major concern at the time, and it was always being discussed, within the missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My conclusion follows from the documents showed to you, and tendered into exhibits here.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: And I can -- I can understand where you would -- you would choose to take that point of view. And I can't -- I can't disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that Croatian side was not prepared to receive the refugees from Western Slavonia back?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That was an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes or not?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: As I say, that was an issue, and I don't know what the Croatian side was or was not prepared to do. I know that that was an issue. I can't speak for the Croatian side. I can't speak for the -- for the RSK side. I can only speak from the position of -- of an independent monitor. But that was an issue; yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it topic of your discussion with Croatia side?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Always. We discussed that on numerous occasions. There was a reluctance on both sides of -- of the conflict to receive displaced persons from the other. I mean, it's -- the -- the situation as we -- as I understood it at the time was that people were being displaced on no notice, based on their ethnicity. Both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I am interested -- interested for the refugees --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- from Western Slavonia. We have many -- many documents indicating that the issue of refugees from Eastern Slavonia was discussed.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. And that's a -- that's a matter of fact. That's history. Yes, I agree. I can't -- I can't elaborate on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me know, did the ECMM or UNPROFOR have any plan for the people in Eastern Slavonia who temporarily occupied those houses after being expelled from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah. That -- in terms of a plan, that -- that is -- that's an UN issue, that's an UN lead on that one. That's not an ECMM lead on that. Ours was a monitor mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of -- are you aware of such plan?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'd have to go back through the documents to look at them again to refresh my memory. I can't speak to you in any detail on it right now. I really can't. I'd like to, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me know, was it inconsistent to insist that Croatian refugees be returned to Eastern Slavonia while no similar accommodation were made for refugees from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know, if you go back to 1992/1993 and you try and understand what was happening at the time, and there was much confusion, there was a great detail of reluctance on all factions, not just -- not just on -- on any one particular side but there was a great -- there was a great reluctance to get this thing moving and ... and I -- both sides were stalling for time, as I understand it. It was a source of frustration. And we were just as frustrated with the Croatian side as we were with the -- with the RSK side or any other faction in theatre at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And whether the Croatian side or UNPROFOR expect -- expect the RSK authorities to re-expel Western Slavonia refugees to Serbia or to live there in open fields?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not aware of -- of -- of any particular plan to that effect. I'm really not. And I would have to go back and refresh my memory by looking at the historical documentation of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we look -- we have Rule 65 ter exhibit 5324. It is paragraph 52. I will read it for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should go to private session. I don't know whether this specific paragraph is confidential or not or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yeah, if I could just help on that front. The provider has asked us to use this document confidentially. So if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have P286 -- 2847, please. It is Resolution 762. It is paragraph 17. I read it for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR believes that there is a direct link between this situation and the presence of large numbers of refugees in these areas. The influx into the UNPAs of Serb refugees from other parts of Croatia, and more recently from Bosnia and Herzegovina, continues unabated. The refugees from Croatia, some of whom appear to foresee no possibility of return to their homes, especially in Western and Central Slavonia, have reportedly occupied houses left vacant by the departure of their non-Serb occupants. While they claim that they are entitled to these houses as long as their own homes are denied to them by the Croatian authorities, the Force Commander is concerned that such actions are part of a concerted effort to change the ethnic composition of these areas." I stop here. Would you tell us, please, how did the ECMM understand this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That was the crux of the problem, that was the crux of the issue that was central to much of what we were attempting to verify, observe, and monitor. So from the perspective of the European Community Monitoring Mission, we would place monitoring teams inside all factions, inside all regions, on both sides of -- of the conflict. And you must have had the opportunity by now to read many of our reports. We tried to provide as objective a view as to what was actually occurring as we could -- as we could honestly -- honestly get, and that -- that's a matter of record and it speaks for itself. That is -- that is the crux of the problem with respect to what is now being termed ethnic cleansing and displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me, please, how would the ethnic composition of the areas change if Serbs from one part of Croatia move into other part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know, I can't answer that because I don't know. But from a -- from the perspective of an international monitoring mission, it would have been our desire to see each faction represent -- or respect the rights of minority groups, whatever their ethnic composition might happen to be. It was a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me know, would the relocation of Serbs from Western Slavonia to former Yugoslavia, Serbia, would change the ethnic composition of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I suppose from a Croatian perspective at the time it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they would like it?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: From a Croatian perspective at the time, probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: But that's just a comment. I mean, I don't know. I can't -- I can't honestly give you an opinion. And it wasn't my role, it wasn't the role of the mission to -- to give opinions on that. It was the role of the mission to facilitate, observe, and report on the -- the developments within the region in -- in trying to find a permanent resolution to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me know if I understand -- if I understand you, Croatia authorities did not like Serbs from Western Slavonia back in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to interject here. The witness has said to the same question effectively, "I don't know, I can't honestly give you an opinion." So the question has been asked an answered, and the witness has recognised that he would speculating on the subjective views of a different party. So we object to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't finish my question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, let's see if what you add to the question could improve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand from all the -- all your answers, there was no -- there was no clear plan to return the Serbs from Western Slavonia -- Serbs from Eastern Slavonia to Western Slavonia. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Okay. Here's what I'm going to say on it. There was a plan but it wasn't universally accepted as being a workable solution and that led to the intransigence that was occurring at the time. But I cannot -- I really cannot see inside the minds of tacticians and strategists from any of the opposing factions, but I can see where you might draw that conclusion. I'm sorry if that doesn't -- that doesn't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your last answer reads that it wasn't -- the plan wasn't universally accepted. But whom -- by whom?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: By any of the factions. By any of the factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It includes Croats?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It includes Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It means that the Croats didn't like to see Serbs from Western Slavonia back. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, you are right in assuming that. But, you know, again, from a -- from the perspective of an international operative, we were interested in seeing the laws of armed conflict respected, the rights of ethnic minorities, on both sides, or all sides, because there were more than just the two sides, respected. And however, you know, these events transpired at the time, doesn't excuse the commission of crimes by one side or another. That's just my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm just interested in the position of the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And if they didn't want the Serbs from Eastern Slavonia back in Western Slavonia, and wanted to resettle Croats into their homes in Eastern Slavonia where were the Serbs from Western Slavonia, the only option is to resettle these people in Yugoslavia or to leave them on the -- in the open fields. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Again, pure speculation. But -- but the -- the response that the international community was looking for at the time was to have all sides sit down and resolve the issue through negotiation. And that wasn't happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have a look at P2677, please. It is paragraph 19. I don't know, is it confidential or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No. This is the UN Secretary-General report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: It's not confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the second sentence in -- I'm interested in first two sentences from paragraph 19. It reads: "Extremist elements on both sides are nevertheless still present in Sector West. The Croatian police have often played an intimidatory role which has vigorously protested by UNPROFOR." Could you explain what that means, intimidatory role?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I don't know. That's an UN document and I'm not here to comment on UN documents, sir. I would have read it. And intimidatory involves intimidation, tactics, methods, and could in today's terms could be interpreted as terrorist, terrorist activities. Intimidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed about such cases?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Of course, yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: But I should say they were happening on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There are a lot of documents in records about it. Could you look at paragraph 20 of this report, please.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment to find this specific sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we go to next page, please. Hmm. Next page. Oh. Sorry. May we go to -- to previous page. It is last sentence, actually, that's spilled to another page. Paragraph 20, please. I read it for the record: "Certain political leaders have sought to develop movements for return to -- to the UNPAs within stated deadlines, and then to organise mass returns. UNPROFOR has emphasised at all levels that the basic conditions of security do not exist for such mass returns and that the highly publicised attempts made so far not only exacerbate tensions but, if persisted in, could lead to renewed tragedies. On one occasion, in the Osijek area on" - may we go to the next page, please - "on 30 September, the situation was made worse by public statements by a senior officer that the Croatian army would support such returns and move up behind the marching people. These events caused great tension in Sector East, which is the displaced persons' stated destination and, indeed, fear among the Serb population in the sector ..." Could you please clarify this statement? Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I do, in fact. And it's a matter of history. It's an accurate statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Today you testified about pink zones.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I know, these zones were almost completely deserted. There was no population in the pink zones, but Croats and Serbs. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: They were being depopulated, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last issue is your -- your very short meeting with Mr. Hadzic and the words about his position told you by your escort.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to clarify. It wasn't a meeting. We bumped into each other as -- as I was -- either he was leaving or I was leaving, but we just passed. And I happened to ask the question, who was this person. I didn't have a meeting with him. I hadn't arranged a meeting with him. It's just that I am aware of who he was through the records, and on that one particular day, we just passed in the hallway. That's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you be able to tell us who was this man who give you information?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: You know, I'm not exactly sure of who it was. I thought it was Lieutenant-Colonel Ray Wolosichuk [phoen], who was with me at the time. And I'm not -- I'm not 100 per cent sure of that. It's a long time ago, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, would you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Wolosichuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Wolosichuk. He was --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: He was a monitor who was assigned to the coordination centre in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From what country is he --

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: He was from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He is also from Canada?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: He is also from Canada. But I'm not sure that it was him because I was visiting there and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your time. Thank you very much. I finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I finish my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Gillett, anything in re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Probably five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about incursions by the Croatian side during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I get 65 ter document 3151 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, this is an UNPROFOR military info summary. Would you have access to these kinds of reports during your time with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yeah, we shared reports back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we go to page 13 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, under the heading 18 September 1992, in the middle of the page, we see a series of incidents listed. Inside the UNPA, we see militia cars tried to force their way through Ken position at Civljane to Peruca. Then under inside pink zones, we see an incident with fire from the CA, which I understand to be Croatian army. In number 2, we see fire from the TDF, which I understand to be Territorial Defence Force side to the Croatian army. And then we see another three incidents of this nature. From your experience, were there incidents and provocations by both sides during this conflict?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could I ask, are you aware what HMG - this is point 2 - means, the acronym?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: HMG is heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Would that be an example of a crew-fired weapon that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: That is a crew-served weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document, 3151, for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2912. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You were also asked about the process of demilitarisation during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 3624 on the monitor, please. And this is a United Nations Secretary-General report. If we could go to paragraph 7 of this report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We see here that it reports: "The justification given by the Knin authorities for these forces that they are needed to defend Serb-controlled areas from attacks and infiltration by the Croatian army. General Nambiar has repeatedly stressed to the authorities in Belgrade and Knin that it is UNPROFOR that exercises the protection function in the UNPAs, and that the presence of these paramilitary units is contrary to the United Nations plan and has caused the Croatian army to retain some of its forces at the confrontation line. As a result, clashes continue to occur along the line, fueling intercommunal tension in the UNPAs." Would the presence of these Serb militia forces in the UNPAs and pink zones constitute a provocation to the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: It was irritant. I'm not sure that "provocation" is a word that I would use because you have to understand that the Serb population was under siege at the time and they saw themselves as being under siege. So that was, again, the issue in trying to get the -- the implementation of the Vance Plan to move forward. So the answer is yes, but I'm trying to understand it from the -- from the Serb side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the reports that you read, how did these armed forces, the Serb militia, treat the non-Serb population within the UNPAs and the pink zones?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a part of my cross-examination, and it was part of witness statement, and it could be matter of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking about this is it relates to the issue of Croatian forces being provoked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now go to paragraph 34 of this report. Thank you. And just for the record, this is one of the paragraphs that was inadvertently cut off in D70, which is a draft version of this report that was admitted. This is the full, final version of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We see here it states that: "The root cause of the deterioration in the UNPAs since late July has been the Knin authorities' decision to create new paramilitary forces. This action is inconsistent with the demilitarisation of the UNPAs and thus is a blatant violation of the United Nations plan." It then continues in the same vein. Would the creation of new paramilitary forces constitute a provocation to the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Final topic. You were asked about the return of refugees and you were referred to document P2677.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get P2677 on the monitor. Paragraph 20, which is page 7. And if we go over to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You were asked about the incident concerning the return of refugees to Osijek, which is in Sector East. And we read that these events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not return to refugees from Osijek. It was the statement of officer in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we read the sentence: "These events caused great tension in Sector East, which was the displaced persons' stated destination, indeed, fear among the Serb population in the sector (for fear, on both sides, is still a factor in the UNPAs). This, in turn, provided both reason and pretext for further mobilisation of the Serb special militias and renewed victimisation of the non-Serb people." Would the potential return of refugees to their homes justify further victimisation of the remaining non-Serbs in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question again. I just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is incomplete quotation or incomplete statement. Because it was said, clearly said, that Croatian army would support such returns and move up behind the marching people. It was not just the refugees but Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Indeed. And that was read in cross-examination. I was reading the passage that wasn't highlighted in cross-examination to give a complete basis for the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, based on that, my question is: Would this paternal -- potential, sorry, return of refugees supported by the Croatian army justify the further victimisation of the non-Serbs who remained in the UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Not in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. I was waiting for the end of the French interpretation before I put my question to you. I would like to go back to the exhibit that you were shown. That was 65 ter 3624 and that was a report by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. I would like to know: Who was supposed to provide protection of the police in UNPA zones in your sector?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand -- do you mean the United Nations police or the local police of the -- of the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the very principle of policing, police protection for people and for goods. Would it be the local police or the UN police?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: The UN police, at the time, were in a mentoring role. They weren't providing protection. As I understand it, they weren't providing protection to anyone. The protection of the civilian population was the responsibility of the local police in the various sectors, according to wherever -- wherever they lived. There were several different police forces, and the UN -- UNCIVPOL were a -- were a mentoring force. As I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. And that's how I understand things as well. But in the report of the UN Secretary-General, we just read that paramilitary forces were created by the Knin authorities which caused difficulties. Now, these forces that were considered as paramilitaries in this report, how did the Knin authorities consider them? Did they consider them as the police or the military? Knowing that it was incumbent upon the Knin authorities to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: I understand your question. I can't comment on what the Knin authorities thought. I can only comment on how we, as an international monitoring force, interpreted the -- their actions. There are two -- a policeman is an officer of the law who operates within the law, who operates as an individual who protects a people, citizens, in accordance with the law. The paramilitary forces that we're talking about that were referred to as "special police," in our view, or in my view, were military-type militias, and that was in contravention of the spirit of the Vance Plan. As I understand it. They were a fairly large force. They were more heavily armed than policemen and they operated in an organised military fashion as opposed to the operations of a civilian police officer in accordance with whatever law he happens to be operating inside. Does that make any sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much. I understood you perfectly well. This force, this special police, that was considered by the report as a paramilitary force, were they alone on the ground for the protection of people and property, or were there, in addition, also local police forces?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: There were local police forces. And those local police forces we, as a -- as a monitoring mission, would consider them to be exactly what they were: Police forces. Policemen. The paramilitaries we considered to be a -- or the special police, we considered them to be a paramilitary force. Perhaps I can -- I can illustrate by stating that a policeman operates under the principle of minimum force, minimum use of force. A paramilitary force operates under the military objective of maximum use of force. One is more intimidating than the other. I hope that clarifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, just one question arising from Your Honours' questions in relation to police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, you've commented on the regular police in response to the -- the final question from Judge Mindua. How were the local or regular police armed in the UNPAs and pink zones?

utterances.speaker: FRED NOSEWORTHY
utterances.text: Civilian police or regular police would be armed with side-arms. And it was not uncommon to see them with short-range long guns, AK-47 type.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Noseworthy, this is the end of your testimony. You are now released as a witness. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal, and we wish you a safe journey back home. The court usher will escort you out of the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there anything else for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
